title: Chapter Thirty-One: Mo
bio: “Mo” — The character joins the radical for “woman” to the graph for “end”; it means the tip, the very end. As the saying goes: where it is stillest, things hang most in the balance.
paragraphs: Two or three days went by, and still nothing from the project office.

Zheng Zhiyong couldn’t sit still in his office. He called Supervisor Zhou twice, and Supervisor Zhou’s tone was even more polite than before: “The leader’s side is still going through the process, Mr. Zheng. Please wait a little longer.” Polite to that degree, it left Zheng Zhiyong all the less sure. He called Cong Shasha and asked whether there was any news from Director Wu.
Cong Shasha said, “No. I sent him a WeChat and he didn’t reply. Let’s wait a bit longer.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “All right.”

After she hung up, Cong Shasha sat on the edge of the bed in her room, phone in hand, the message she’d sent still lit up on the screen. She stared at it a while, then put the phone down. She seemed to know what Director Wu was waiting for. And she knew what she was waiting for too.

On the afternoon of the third day, her phone rang. A WeChat from Director Wu, just one line: “Little Cong, if you’re free this weekend, let’s go out and have some fun. There’s a hot spring outside Beijing — I’ve got a free guest voucher.”
Cong Shasha looked at that line for a long time. She had stayed on in Beijing the whole while precisely to wait for this message. What had to come, it seemed, had come after all.
She replied with one word: “Okay.”

Early Saturday morning she followed the address Director Wu had given her and took a taxi north. Out past the city proper to Changping, onto the expressway, then onto a small road lined with poplars on both sides, and finally the car stopped at the gate of a compound. It wasn’t big. A wooden sign hung by the gate reading “Still Water Lodge,” the characters carved by hand, the paint flaking a little. A few old pagoda trees grew in the courtyard, their branches bare, with two or three cars parked beneath them. An attendant led her through the front hall and on toward the back, through a moon gate, and inside was an open-air hot spring — not a big pool, edged with stone, white steam rising off the surface. A few loungers stood beside the pool. No one was there.

Director Wu was already soaking. He leaned back against the stones at the edge of the pool, arms draped over the rim, his face flushed red from the steam. When he saw Cong Shasha coming, he smiled and said, “Little Cong, you’re here. Go change and come down for a soak. The water’s good.”
Cong Shasha said, “Director Wu, I just came to keep you company. I didn’t even bring a swimsuit.”
Director Wu said, “They’ve got everything here. The front desk sells them — go pick one out and put it on the room bill. Room 118.”

Cong Shasha had no choice but to go buy a swimsuit at the front desk, then went into the changing room and put it on, wrapped a bathrobe over it, walked to the pool, took off the robe and got in. The water was very hot. She let herself get used to it before sitting down across from Director Wu. There were a meter or two between them, and the steam rising up blurred their faces a little.

It was a private bath within a public area. There wasn’t a soul anywhere to be seen around them, just the two of them, very quiet, and the gurgle of the spring water bubbling up. After about ten minutes like this, Director Wu said, “Little Cong, that tea you gave me last time — I opened it when I got home.”
Cong Shasha said, “Do you like it all right?”

Director Wu looked at her and smiled. It wasn’t the same smile as at the dinner last time. There was a bit of “So you’re playing this game with me” in it, but it wasn’t entirely annoyed either. He said, “Little Cong, the tea’s nice enough — pre-Qingming green tea. But putting things in the tea, that’s not so good. If I accepted it, I’d be making a mistake. I’ve brought the thing with me. You take it back with you in a while, and we’ll say it never happened.”
Cong Shasha said, “Director Wu, I didn’t mean anything by it. I just thought that little thing wasn’t worth mentioning specially.”
Director Wu smiled. “Don’t go learning bad ways so young, eh?”
Cong Shasha said nothing.
Director Wu put on his bathrobe and said, “Come on, come back to my room with me and take the thing away.”

Shasha put on her bathrobe too and followed Director Wu timidly through several corridors into a small, private, self-contained courtyard — Director Wu’s room. It was a suite: sofas and a coffee table in the outer room, the bedroom inside. The curtains were drawn, and the light was dim and heavy.

Shasha stood shyly off to one side of the outer room. Director Wu came out of the bedroom carrying that familiar black velvet pouch, put it on the coffee table, motioned for Shasha to sit on the sofa by the table, then pushed the black velvet pouch toward Cong Shasha. He said, “Your company’s qualifications were in order to begin with. The contract process can start next Monday. Take the thing back. This isn’t the way to do this.”
Cong Shasha looked at the velvet pouch. It seemed to have gotten a little wet; a small dark patch had soaked into the surface of the velvet.
She didn’t reach out for it.
Director Wu said, “Little Cong, you were with Ms. Diao at Yuanwang for seven years. You ought to know that between her and me, it isn’t things like this that get matters done.”

Cong Shasha crossed her hands to hold the collar of her bathrobe closed, raised her head and looked at him. She said, “Director Wu, I don’t know what to do either. Teach me. I only want to get things done. You can see I’m not very old — I’ve never been married, never even had a boyfriend, I’ve got no experience of anything. If you’re willing to teach a schoolgirl, I’ll certainly be a humble student.”
Director Wu’s expression moved.
Cong Shasha said, “Director, I’ve been forward. I truly, sincerely want to be friends with you. If you think the gift wasn’t appropriate, I apologize — or maybe I shouldn’t have come today at all.”
Director Wu looked at her for a good while, then laughed.
He said, “Little Cong, the things you say. If I didn’t want to be friends with you, we wouldn’t even have had that first dinner.”

Cong Shasha said, “Director Wu, I know that, that’s just it. So I never thought of treating you as an outsider. If I’ve done something wrong, please forgive me. If you can’t accept the thing, I’ll take it back. What I should do — you teach me. I don’t know how to do anything, but I can learn.”
Director Wu didn’t speak right away.
Cong Shasha said nothing more. The two of them sat on the sofas on either side of the coffee table, a meter apart. A bird sang in the little courtyard, sang twice, and then stopped.

Director Wu leaned back against the sofa, moved his shoulder, frowned, and reached up to rub his right shoulder. He said, “Maybe I’m getting old. A good long soak in the hot spring and my shoulders and back still haven’t loosened up. The old injury here in my neck and shoulder hurts even sitting down.”

Shasha, at the other end of the sofa with her head bowed like a child who’d done something wrong, looked up at this and said, “Director Wu, my dad has a bad neck and shoulders. I’ve been massaging him since I was little — I’m practically a pro. If you don’t mind, let me give you a rub.”

Director Wu said, “Have you massage me? That wouldn’t be proper. This is an old complaint of mine. From sitting in an office — this bit of the right shoulder, frozen shoulder. Not much you can do for it except rest it. And who has time to rest?”

Cong Shasha looked at him. She knew very well what she was going to do next, and knew very well what taking this step would mean. She’d followed Diao Kexin for seven years and watched how, at moments like this, Diao Kexin would hold her words back, let her eyes go soft, lean her body forward just a little. She’d learned it, learned it for a long time; it was only that she’d never met anyone worth using all of it on.
Now that someone was sitting right in front of her, rubbing his own shoulder.
She stood up, went around behind him and said, “Director Wu, what’s the big deal? Let me give you a massage. I’m a pro — try it and you’ll see.”
Director Wu turned his head and glanced at her, didn’t refuse, and said, “Let’s try it, then.”

One in front and one behind, the two of them went into the inner bedroom of the suite. Director Wu lay face down on the bed and undid his bathrobe. Cong Shasha sat sideways on the edge of the bed, turned and put her hands on his right shoulder. His shoulder was very hard, the muscle pulled tight; she could feel the stiff knot. She pressed down with her thumb, and Director Wu let out a hiss. “Yes, right there.”

She pressed for a while, her fingers moving up along the line of his neck and shoulder, pressing both sides of his neck, then the hollow below the back of his head. Director Wu’s breathing slowly eased, and his shoulders sank a little. He said, “Little Cong, this skill of yours — you really are a pro.”
Cong Shasha said, “Told you. My dad’s shoulders were bad too, and I’ve been giving him massages since I was little.”
Director Wu said, “A good daughter.”

Cong Shasha didn’t reply. Her fingers were still on the back of his neck. She could feel his body heat, could feel that the skin on his neck was a little loose — the skin of a man past fifty. There was a place in her heart that was cold, like a stone sunk at the bottom, not moving. Another place was calculating — how far this step had come, how to take the next one. Because both her arms were working so hard, the tie of her bathrobe had come loose, showing the two-piece swimsuit underneath, and Shasha drew her hands back to retie the robe.

Before Cong Shasha could pull her hands back, Director Wu caught hold of one. He raised himself up, pulled her hand around to the front and held it in his own, rolled over and pressed Shasha’s hand against his chest.

Cong Shasha’s bathrobe had fallen completely open now, and she had no hand free to tie it. So, following where Director Wu’s hand led her, she began pressing on his bare chest and belly. His swim trunks were wet and tight below, and Director Wu’s hand was guiding hers on downward. She went where he guided her.
Director Wu saw that her eyes were very calm — so calm that it rather surprised him.
He said, “You and Ms. Diao really are different.”
Cong Shasha said, “Director Wu, I told you — I’m not using you as my gun.”

Director Wu smiled. He reached out and pulled her onto the bed, letting Shasha lie on his chest. Shasha lay on top of him, and he took the chance to wrap his arms around her and draw her closer. Cong Shasha didn’t pull away; instead she lay obediently on his chest.

The gauze curtain in the inner room was drawn; light came through it, but you couldn’t see the courtyard wall. The big bed under the window was made up with pure white sheets, and the light in the room was soft. Director Wu lay still and let Shasha lie on his chest, and neither of them spoke or moved.

But her mind didn’t stop for a second. She remembered that night in the fourth-floor dormitory, Zheng Zhiyong standing by the table, opening the takeout boxes one by one and turning them out into the bone china, setting them out so neatly, as if afraid of spilling the soup. She remembered him coming back from town the next day, pushing that black velvet pouch in front of her and saying, “Two of the hundred-gram ones. You take these for now, and if it’s not enough, we’ll see.” She remembered how, when he said “I know,” his voice was very flat — so flat it was as if he’d pressed something down.
And then she thought of Diao Kexin.

Diao Kexin, back then, had probably come through this same way. In Gao Fei’s hotel room, in the back seat of a client’s car, in some place she could no longer remember — she’d done the same thing. Now there was a stone in her own heart, and there was probably one in Diao Kexin’s too. It was just that Diao Kexin had later ground her stone smooth, ground it into a tool, ground it into a step for climbing upward.
Cong Shasha thought: I won’t grind it smooth. I’ll let it dig into me. As long as it digs in, I’ll know who I am.
Suddenly Director Wu began taking off Shasha’s bathrobe, and took off his own wet trunks. Shasha’s two-piece swimsuit, part of its water soaked up by the robe, clung tight to her body.
Director Wu reached out. The strap of the swimsuit slipped off her shoulder, and then he peeled off the boy-shorts bottom Shasha was wearing.

Shasha didn’t move, didn’t struggle, let him take hold of her and press her down beneath him. She felt his hands on her body, a little rough, a little heavy. Felt his breath against her ear, a little stale, a little hot. Then Director Wu took a condom out from under the pillow and put it on. Then his body pressed down on her, and for an instant her chest felt tight, as if something were blocking it.
She closed her eyes.
Director Wu moved a little faster. Cong Shasha turned her face away and pressed it to the pillow.
She counted in her head. When she got to seventy, Director Wu stopped.
He got off her and lay beside her, breathing hard for a few breaths. The room was quiet for a while, with only the hum of the air-conditioning vent.
Cong Shasha spoke first. She said, “Director Wu, your shoulder doesn’t hurt anymore, does it?”
Director Wu gave a laugh and said, “Call me big brother. I’ll call you Shasha.”

Cong Shasha turned on her side and looked at him. There was no hurt on her face, no embarrassment, nothing at all. Just a calm face, as if she were sitting in an ordinary meeting. The two of them lay quietly in each other’s arms, no kissing, no talking, lying there calm and comfortable, the temperature pleasant, the air tranquil.
Director Wu looked at that face of hers for a while and said, “Rest a bit, take a shower, and in a little while I’ll take you for a good meal.”
Cong Shasha said, “Thank you, Director Wu.”
Director Wu said, “I told you, call me big brother. Shasha, from now on, if there’s ever anything you need, you can come straight to me.”
Cong Shasha said, “Okay.”

She got up and went to the bathroom to shower. Hot water poured over her. She stood under the showerhead with her eyes closed, stood there a long time. The water ran down her face, into her mouth, a little salty. She didn’t know whether it was water or something else.

When she came out, Director Wu was already dressed, sitting on the sofa in the outer room drinking tea. The black velvet pouch was no longer on the coffee table. Cong Shasha glanced at the table and didn’t ask.

Director Wu said, “I’ve had them prepare lunch.” The two of them had a lavish private-kitchen meal in the little courtyard. Shasha’s own clothes were still in the locker in the public bathhouse, so she wore the bathrobe from Director Wu’s room the whole time. After lunch Director Wu told Shasha about some of his past and his life, and Shasha felt that the man did have quite a lot that was out of the ordinary about him.
When they’d finished lunch, Director Wu said, “Why don’t you stay here tonight? I have to rush back to the city this evening — I’ve got an important dinner.”
Cong Shasha said, “Big brother, I won’t stay either. I’ll head back to Xi’an as soon as I can.”
Director Wu said, “All right then, I’ll have my driver take you first.”

She walked out of the room, along the gravel path, through the moon gate, across the front hall, back to the public bathhouse to change into her own clothes, and then back out into the courtyard. Director Wu’s driver was already waiting by the car and opened the door for her.

She got into the car. It pulled out onto that little road lined with poplars. She took out her phone and sent Zheng Zhiyong a WeChat: “Brother Yong, the thing’s been accepted. It’ll be taken care of next week.”
Zheng Zhiyong replied very quickly: “Good, Shasha. Thank you for all your trouble. Head back to Xi’an as soon as you can.”
Cong Shasha looked at the message for a few seconds, then turned the phone over, face down on her lap, leaned back in the seat and closed her eyes.

She didn’t say anything else. Didn’t say anything about the hot spring, didn’t say anything about the room, didn’t say anything about the shoulder, didn’t say anything about the seventy-odd counts. She pressed all of it down to the bottom of her heart and put it alongside that stone.

The car headed into the city. Beijing in March: the poplars by the road hadn’t budded yet, their bare branches jabbing up under the gray-blue sky. Cong Shasha looked out the window and thought: Diao Kexin, back then, probably came through it this way too. Send a WeChat, say “It’s done,” and swallow everything else.
She thought: I’ve swallowed it. When she got back to Xi’an, she went to her rented place and didn’t go into the office.

Three days later, notice came from the Sixth Academy’s project office. The supplementary verification had passed, and the contract process was starting. Supervisor Zhou’s tone on the phone was a lot lighter: “Mr. Zheng, congratulations. You can sign the contract next week.”

When Zheng Zhiyong hung up, he sat in his office and didn’t smile right away. He thought the whole thing through from beginning to end. Cong Shasha had gone to see Director Wu, and after she came back she told him, “The thing’s been accepted, he says it’ll be taken care of next week.” He hadn’t asked for details. Cong Shasha hadn’t told him any either. There was a tacit understanding between the two of them, like putting something into a box and closing the lid, and neither of them would touch it.

Suddenly he believed again what Diao Kexin had once told him: once they accept the goods, you don’t have to give them your body. But it had never occurred to him that there were also times when, without trust first built through the body, the goods couldn’t be accepted at all.

The contract was signed by passing it around for signatures. That day Zheng Zhiyong called Shasha, who hadn’t shown up for several days, to come in to the office to see him. Shasha had made herself up carefully, her hair pinned up, light makeup on her face. When she walked into Zheng Zhiyong’s office, Zheng Zhiyong looked at her. The smile on her face was perfectly proper, no different from that of any normal, capable sales director.
After the contract was signed, Zheng Zhiyong took the team out to dinner. During the meal he raised his glass and said to Cong Shasha, “Shasha, you’ve done a great service on this order.”
Cong Shasha raised her glass, clinked it against his, and said, “Mr. Zheng, it’s everyone’s achievement.”

In public she always said “Mr. Zheng,” not “Brother Yong,” and never once got it wrong. Zheng Zhiyong glanced at her and said nothing. When Shasha went to the restroom, Zheng Zhiyong followed her out and asked her quietly whether she wanted to come to his place tonight. Shasha nodded.

That night, after the dinner broke up, Old Zheng and Shasha walked back to the company and up to the fourth floor. Cong Shasha sat on the sofa, took off her heels, put her feet on the carpet and let out a long breath. Zheng Zhiyong sat down beside her, and the two of them were silent for a while.
Zheng Zhiyong said, “Shasha, are you all right?”
Cong Shasha said, “I’m fine. We’ve got the project, so everything after this will be easier.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “I’m not asking about the project.”
Cong Shasha turned her head and glanced at him. She smiled, a very faint smile, so faint it was almost invisible. She said, “Brother Yong, I’m fine. What are you thinking?”
Zheng Zhiyong looked at her for a good while. He wanted to say something; his mouth opened, then closed again.

Cong Shasha stood up, went to the window and looked out at the man-made water features in the park. The streetlamps’ light fell on the water and broke into pieces. She said, “Brother Yong, let me tell you something.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “Tell me.”
Cong Shasha said, “Brother Yong, Xinghuan has to get big. Bigger than Yuanwang. You promised me.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “I promise you.”
Cong Shasha nodded, took his hand from her shoulder, squeezed it once and let it go. She said, “Then I’m going to shower. We’ve got a meeting with the supply-chain people tomorrow.”
She went into the bathroom and shut the door. Zheng Zhiyong stood at the window, listening to the sound of water from inside.

He suddenly thought: was Diao Kexin like this too, back then? At Gao Fei’s side, on the one hand being his sales director, taking cities and seizing ground for him, on the other hand being his woman, tumbling with him in bed? The script was so familiar, as if it were playing out again on him.

When Cong Shasha came out of the bathroom she had changed into her pajamas, her hair blown dry and hanging loose over her shoulders. She saw Zheng Zhiyong standing by the window smoking, went over, put her arms around his waist from behind and laid her face against his back.
Zheng Zhiyong stubbed out his cigarette in the drink can on the windowsill, turned around and took her in his arms. Her body was very soft against him; he could feel her breathing, even and steady.
He lowered his head and kissed her lips gently.

Cong Shasha’s lips were cool at first, with a little of the steam from the bathroom still on them; after he’d kissed her twice they slowly warmed. Her hands rose from his waist to the back of his neck, her fingertips slipping into his hair, pressing once, not too hard and not too light. Zheng Zhiyong’s kiss went from light to hard; his tongue parted her lips and probed inside. Cong Shasha made a little “mm” sound, pressed her body forward and pushed her chest against him.

Holding her, he took two steps back, and her back bumped against the frame of the screen; the screen swayed. The bump made Cong Shasha give a soft little cry, and he took the chance to draw her whole body into his arms, his hand slipping in under the hem of her pajamas and finding the smooth skin at her waist. Her waist was very slender, a little hot against his palm. His hand went up, found her back, found the thin strap under her pajama top, then went down again and found the hollow at the small of her back.

Cong Shasha’s hands went downward too and found his belt. She tugged at it twice without getting it undone and gave it an impatient yank. Zheng Zhiyong gave a low laugh and freed one hand to help her; the buckle came loose with a click. She pulled his shirt out of his waistband and ran her hand up his belly. Her palm was a little cool against his burning skin, and his breath went heavy.

He picked her up. Cong Shasha’s legs wrapped naturally around his waist, and he held her up by her bottom and carried her from the screen to the bed — two steps, then one step back. Her back touched the edge of the bed, and she tipped backward and fell onto the dark gray comforter, her hair fanning out across the pillow.

Zheng Zhiyong bent down and kissed her from her lips to her chin, to her neck. Her neck was very sensitive; the moment he touched it she tipped her head back, and a very soft, held-down sound came from her throat. His hand pushed her pajama top all the way up from the hem, bunching it at her chest and baring her body underneath — she wore nothing under it. The light was very dim, but it was enough for him to see. He bent his head and kissed her there.

Cong Shasha’s hands gripped his hair, her fingers tightening and loosening, tightening and loosening. Her breathing went ragged, her chest rising and falling fast. She tugged at his shirt, tugged twice, and said, “Take it off.”

He straightened up, pulled off his shirt and threw it on the floor. Cong Shasha sat up too, pulled the pajama top bunched at her chest off over her head and tossed it aside. She reached to undo his trousers, and he helped her get them off. When the two of them came together again, skin against skin, both were burning.

Zheng Zhiyong looked down at her. Her face was flushed, her eyes half open and half closed, her lashes casting a small shadow in the dim light. He kissed her neck; she tipped her head back, lifting her chin, and a very soft, blurred syllable came from her throat.

His hand went lower, along the side of her waist, and stopped at her hipbone. Her body moved, as if answering. He went on lower; she caught his wrist — didn’t push it away, only held it for a moment, then let go.

After that, neither of them said much. There was only the rustle of fabric in the room and the two of them breathing heavier and heavier. The strip of light from the gap in the curtains lay across the carpet and didn’t reach the bed. Her fingers left a few faint marks on his back — they didn’t hurt, but he could feel them.
She rolled on top and pinned him beneath her, her hair falling and sweeping across his chest. She bent down, pressed her forehead to his, and said, “Brother Yong.”
He said, “Mm.”
She said, “Look at me.”
He looked at her.
She said, “It’s me now.”
He said nothing, reached up and pulled her head down and kissed her. She bit his lip, very lightly, not hurting — as if leaving a mark.

Of what came after, what he remembered was that her hands never let go — gripping his wrists, or resting on his shoulders, or clasped at the back of his neck. He remembered her breathing going from quick to long, and from long to quick again. He remembered that at one point she said something, very low, and he didn’t catch it. He remembered that in his last stretch there was nothing at all in his head — empty, clean, as if someone had rinsed it through with water.
When it was over, the two of them lay side by side, catching their breath for a while. The ceiling light wasn’t on, and the strip of light from the curtain gap still lay across the carpet.
Cong Shasha spoke first. She said, “What were you thinking just now?”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “Nothing. It was empty.”
Cong Shasha gave a laugh and said, “Empty’s good.”
Zheng Zhiyong said nothing more. He reached out and drew her head over to rest on his chest. She lay there a while, and her breathing slowly evened out, as if she were falling asleep.

He lay in the dark looking at the ceiling. What had emptied out of him a moment ago was slowly coming back now. He thought of Diao Kexin, of Zhang Jingyu, of Director Wu, of those two gold bars, of the look on Cong Shasha’s face the day she came back from Beijing, with no expression on it at all. He thought of her saying, “It’s me now.” When she said it, her voice was very steady and her eyes very direct. He hadn’t thought about it much at the time; now, thinking back, he didn’t quite dare to follow where it led, the thing pressed down beneath those words.

He rolled over to face her. Her eyes were closed, her lashes perfectly still in the dim light. He looked at her a while, then gently lifted her hand from his chest, laid it on the covers, and tucked the covers in around her.
She stirred and said drowsily, “Brother Yong, turn off the light.”
He said, “The light’s off.”
She said “Oh” and fell asleep.
Zheng Zhiyong closed his eyes.
Outside the window, the Xi’an night was as still as ever.
